units.translation: a thing suspended and driven by the winds

Scholium: ὥσπερ εἴδωλον κρεμάμενον ὑπὸ τὸν ἀέρα [like a phantom hanging in the air]. Eustathius mentions it at p. 472, 44; 865, 28; 957, 21, himself also interpreting it as ἀέριον εἴδωλον [an airy phantom]. See κινύσσω.
But now, wretched one, I have suffered an airy phantom, a delight to my enemies.
like a phantom hanging in the air

unless μινύρονται [they lament] should be written with L. Dindorf, comparing the gloss of Hesychius μινύρονται: προφωνοῦσι, προλέγουσι [they announce, they foretell]. The same author explains κινύρεσθαι [to lament] as θρηνεῖν, κλαίειν [to mourn, to weep].
they lament: they announce, they foretell

Thus Turnebus, except that he had written μὴ κινυσσόμην [lest I should move] neglecting the augment. In M κηνυσσόμην [I was moving], an ancient error, as the glosses of the grammarians show: Hesychius κηνυσσόμην: εἴδωλον ἐγινόμην [I became a phantom]. κήνυγμα: τὸ κενὸν τοῦ σώματος, οἷον σκιὰ καὶ εἴδωλον, φάντασμα ἀσθενές καὶ ἀχρεῖον [the emptiness of the body, like a shadow and a phantom, a weak and useless apparition]. Photius κήνυγμα: σκιὰ καὶ εἴδωλον [shadow and phantom]. And the scholiast: ἐφανταζόμην · κήνυγμα (κήνυμα M) γὰρ τὸ εἴδωλον [I was appearing as a phantom; for κήνυγμα is the phantom].
so that, being without a chariot, I might not move.
κηνυσσόμην: I became a phantom. κήνυγμα: the emptiness of the body, like a shadow and a phantom, a weak and useless apparition
I was appearing as a phantom; for κήνυγμα (κήνυμα M) is the phantom
was the title of a satyr play by Aeschylus
Thus Hermann for κιρκηλάτου τ᾽ [and of the hawk-driven].
hawks not far behind the doves
I see a hawk rushing on wings in swift flight
in fear of the hawks of the same wing
he brandishes the wing of a white-rumped hawk
to bind with a circular bond, to hoop
I bind with a circular bond, I hoop
Κισθήνη: Ισοκράτης Πανηγυρικῷ [Cisthene: Isocrates in the Panegyricus] (p. 72d) ὄρος τῆς Θράκης [a mountain of Thrace].
πεδία Κισθήνης [the plains of Cisthene] therefore are the plains near that mountain.
to the Gorgonean plains of Cisthene
"And from there you will come to the ends of the earth and see the mountain of Cisthene."
Euripides in the Licymnius, indicating that Apollo and Liber are one and the same god, writes.

Σαβαῖος [Sabazius] Barnesius on Eurip. Bacch. 408. Cf. Lobeck. Aglaoph. p. 80. The very ancient Vatican codex (1605) has ΟΒΑΚΣΙΟΣ. Perhaps therefore it should be written, in Bacchiac metre, ὁ κισσεὺς Ἀπόλλων ὁ Βάκχος θ᾽ ὁ [the ivy-crowned Apollo, the Bacchus and the] (ὁ Βακχεὺς ὁ [the Bacchic one] Nauck. ὁ Βακχᾶς ὁ [the Bacchic one] the same in Add. p. XIV) μάντις [prophet].
"Master, lover of laurel, Bacchus, Paean, Apollo of the beautiful lyre."
"The ivy-crowned Apollo, the Cabaean, the prophet."
the ivy-crowned Apollo, the Bacchus and the (the Bacchic one
